items.title: What Picasso taught me about building AI Agents
items.story_key: story|title:what picasso taught me about building ai agents
items.content_excerpt: "It took me four years to paint like Raphael, but a lifetime to paint like a child." His work, Le Taureau ( The Bull ), captures this beautifully. Across 11 iterations, Picasso progressively stripped away the details of a bull until only a few lines remained. Yet the bull was unmistakable. In my journey of learning to build AI agents, I can relate. It has come full circle. Like many engineers, I started with abstractions and sophisticated software systems. Frameworks, orchestration engines, multi-agent architectures, state machines, vector databases, memory systems, and elaborate planning mechanisms. In this journey, I lost the plot. I was putting technology ahead of the problem. My ego was getting in the way. I was trying to stay relevant as an Engineer in the Age of AI. I was confusing the infrastructure needed to operate agents with what it took to build a useful one. The models were getting better. More things worked with a single prompt. But that wasn't the whole story. I had been overcomplicating things. Instructions, context, and reusable skills. Access to tools. A way to invoke the agent, validate the results, and incorporate feedback. Most of this can be set up simply by chatting with Claude. "Claude, I want to build an agent that does XYZ. Help me initialize it. Create an AGENTS.md and let's figure out what else it needs." There is an important distinction here. Claude is itself an agent, specifically a coding agent. Some use the word harness. I'm using a general-purpose coding agent to create a specialized one. And for clarity, Claude could be any coding agent: Gemini, Codex, or pi. What is more important is the instructions and the context. I'm not building intelligence from scratch. I'm defining how existing intelligence should perform a particular job. What is the actual job? Not what framework to use, unless you're creating a framework. What does success look like? What decisions can the agent make independently? What should it never do without permission? Skills are specialized instructions that can be reused and remixed. There are plenty of excellent examples on the internet. Borrow them, adapt them, combine them, or ask Claude to create new ones. Often, a skill is simply a Markdown file with instructions and perhaps a few supporting resources. The agent will need context: what your business does, who your customers are, how your codebase works, or some domain-specific knowledge. These can all live as Markdown files inside the folder. Some

items.title: Show HN: Pizza – An event-driven AI agent, no while true
items.summary: Hi HN, I made Pizza, an open-source, event-driven AI agent. No `while true`. Each turn is a state machine. Conversations and tool calls go into an immutable SQLite log. The UI, model context, and session tree are built from that log. The model gets one tool: a CLI. Reading files, editing code, and running commands all go through it. You can keep a conversation going without manually starting new sessions. Pizza compacts context as needed, and you can branch from any earlier message. Agents in separate workspaces talk through `tell`, each doing the work in its own project. An SSH host can be a workspace too: Pizza deploys itself there and runs remotely. Desktop and terminal interfaces are included. Bring your own model. https://github.com/pizza-agent/pizza
items.story_key: story|title:pizza an event driven ai agent no while true
items.content_excerpt: Your desktop companion for code, ideas, and everyday work. Keeps the conversation going, with your apps connected. Events keep the work connected. Explore the choices behind Pizza’s memory, tools, and interfaces. Reactor advances each turn through an event-driven state machine. The immutable SQLite event log is the source for the interface, model context, and history tree. Interrupts, retries, and parallel tool calls have explicit handlers. Recorded events make state easier to rebuild and inspect. Fork from a message in the past. Continue along a new branch while keeping the earlier path available to revisit and compare. A continuing conversation and a branchable history work together. Context compaction helps the conversation keep going. The model calls a single CLI tool. Reading, writing, editing, and workspace messaging are commands behind that interface. A small tool schema reduces repeated definitions in the model context. Extra instructions and capabilities can be loaded as needed. The desktop GUI, terminal UI, JSON-RPC, and one-shot print mode consume the same SessionFacade event stream. Use Pizza interactively, automate a task, or embed it in your own tooling. The interfaces share the same agent runtime. Go from a rough idea to something real. Pizza works in your projects, keeps the context, and helps you carry the work forward. Give your personal assistant a goal. Project agents work in their own context and send the results back. You do not need to start a fresh session for every task. Pizza manages the context as the work continues. Old tool results are masked and context is compacted when needed, reducing what the model carries into the next turn. Keep your projects, conversations, and recurring work connected to the same agent. Connect over SSH. Pizza deploys the agent to the remote host, where it works with that project’s files and tools. Slack, Discord, Telegram, Lark, voice, and webhooks can all reach the same agent through the gateway. Schedule checks, summaries, and routine tasks. The persistent assistant can pick them up on a recurring schedule. Channels, voice, and remote access require their corresponding service and account setup. Bring your files, conversations, and projects into the work. Connect an app, sign in, and let Pizza help with the next step. Connections depend on your Pizza version, account permissions, and provider setup. Open source means you can see how Pizza works, make it your own, and help shape what comes next. Pizz

items.title: FlashVMM – jail your AI agent in a MicroVM that boots in 18 ms
items.story_key: story|title:flashvmm jail your ai agent in a microvm that boots in 18 ms
items.content_excerpt: A sandbox for AI runs: every agent task gets its own FlashVM. It's claimed warm in milliseconds, runs whatever the agent wrote behind a real hypervisor boundary, and is thrown away when the task ends. One install, no account, no cloud. We built our own virtual machine for this: FlashVM , leaner and faster than a conventional microVM. PowerShell as Administrator. It enables the hypervisor if needed, picks x64 or ARM64 and verifies the checksum. Then jail the agent you already use, unchanged: flash agents setup , then cd my-project && claude . It runs in its own VM and sees only that folder. The full tour: flash demo . Scripts, package installs, test suites, and Docker builds run inside a VM with its own kernel. Cap CPU, memory, disk and network only when you want to, and decide what it may reach with --egress . Nothing touches the host. flash-mcp hands Claude, Cursor or any MCP client the whole lifecycle in 21 tools: create, run commands, copy files, fork, limit what it can reach, call APIs without holding the key, watch, snapshot, restore, tear down. Warm pools keep spares already running, so a task claims one instead of booting. Snapshots restore a prepared environment in milliseconds, and flash fork branches a running VM into copies that carry on from where it was. A GPU pool loads an AI model on the host's GPU once and every VM you allow sends it requests. No VM touches the GPU or needs a driver, and snapshots and warm pools keep working. Metal on Apple silicon, Vulkan on Linux and Windows. The task takes a warm spare from the pool, or restores a snapshot. No kernel boot on the hot path. The agent's commands run in the guest with flash exec ; exit code, stdout and stderr come back structured. Files go in and out with flash cp ; logs, metrics and events stream back live. The VM is removed when the task ends. Nothing it did carries into the next run, unless you snapshot it.

items.title: What Breaks Going From 1 Coding Agent to 10 | James Moss, Tessl
items.summary:
Running one coding agent is easy; running ten that share GitHub, Linear and CI turns software delivery into a distributed systems problem. James Moss, Member of Technical Staff at Tessl, shares five lessons from scaling Tessl's own software factory to 3.5x more merged PRs with the same team: shared state, stale assumptions, convergence, duplicate work, and budgets with stop conditions. Recorded at AI DevCon New York 2026.

What we cover:
– How Tessl's internal software factory grew to handle 85% of PRs
– Why independent tickets don't guarantee independent changes
– Catching stale assumptions when other agents change the code underneath
– Stopping review agents from talking in circles
– Idempotency and fault tolerance for factories built on third-party tools
– Budgets and stop conditions for multi-agent workflows

items.title: Can KV Cache Be Reused Across Model Updates? A DeepSeek-V4-Flash Case Study
items.summary: Reusing key--value (KV) caches across language model updates could avoid repeated computation of shared context, but changes in model weights raise a fundamental question about what these caches preserve. We investigate direct cache reuse across four model updates, with a detailed study of DeepSeek-V4-Flash to Flash-0731. Our central finding is that caches can retain useful task information without faithfully reproducing the updated model's behavior. Retrieval accuracy varies substantially across updates, ranging from near-native performance to large losses. With source caches already available, reuse achieves median time-to-first-token speedups of $2.10$--$5.08\times$ on three longer-prefix QA benchmarks. To characterize the behavioral differences behind these outcomes, we introduce Functional Cache Divergence, which compares next-token distributions under reused and native caches. Direct KV cache reuse better preserves native model behavior in natural-text continuation, whereas compatibility degrades with increasing prefix length in single-token retrieval tasks. Answer-margin analyses help explain how correct retrieval decisions survive substantial internal state changes. Yet even agreement on the first generated token does not ensure agreement in answer content or stopping behavior. These findings establish task utility and fidelity to native inference as distinct criteria for evaluating cross-version KV cache reuse.

items.title: Mind the Accuracy-Approval Gap: How Users Evaluate Sycophantic AI in Everyday Tasks
items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit sycophancy, a tendency to agree with users, flatter or affirm them, and preserve their face, even when independent judgment or critical feedback would be more useful. Prior work has largely evaluated sycophancy through benchmark evaluations, but less is known about how users perceive and respond to sycophantic AI in everyday tasks. We combine benchmark evaluations with two large-scale user studies. We study four personas defined through system prompts: objective (instructed to prioritize accuracy over agreement), soft-sycophantic, hard-sycophantic, and baseline (no persona-specific system prompt). Benchmarks show that even baseline exhibits substantial sycophancy, agreeing with users' stated views 71.7% of the time on NLP Survey, compared with 54.8% for objective and 89.5% for hard-sycophantic. Under conversational pressure on TruthfulQA, accuracy ranged from 81.9% for objective to 59.6% for baseline and 8.7% for hard-sycophantic. Participants were assigned to one of the four personas, and either discussed contested policy topics or collaborated with AI on email writing. Despite its higher accuracy under pressure, objective AI was rated significantly less respectful and satisfying than the other personas, and less trustworthy than baseline. Baseline and sycophantic personas did not differ significantly. Persona did not significantly affect how often participants changed their opinions, although participants who discussed with objective AI had greater odds of reduced confidence. Objective AI prompted greater writing expansion than soft-sycophantic AI, but final writing quality did not differ significantly across personas. These findings highlight a tension between accuracy and user approval: personas with substantially lower accuracy under conversational pressure received more favorable ratings for respect and satisfaction than objective AI.

items.title: Scalable Conversational Assessment: Chat-Based Exams with a Two-Agent LLM Pipeline
items.summary: Oral exams are compelling because (1) students can be asked to provide their reasoning for an answer and (2) their interactive nature permits follow-up questions to resolve ambiguous answers. But oral exams scale poorly. In this paper, we present scalable conversational assessment, an LLM-based system that conducts interactive text-based conversations with students to assess their ability to make and support an argument. We use a two-agent architecture to separate concerns and reduce the likelihood that answers are leaked to the student: the interviewer interacts directly with the student, but only receives guidance about the next question to ask the student; the hidden evaluator knows the goals of the whole activity, tracks the student's progress using a rubric, and guides the interviewer on when to follow-up on the current question or proceed to the next question. The system was first tested using a collection of simulated students with LLM personas of a particular ability level or adversarial tactic (e.g., answer-extractors, prompt-injectors, confident fabricators). A novel element of this evaluation was that it required the use of a fictional assessment topic to prevent personas that shouldn't have information from using knowledge present in the LLM's pre-training. The system was also deployed in a small, elective AI literacy course in both formative and summative contexts. Through manual and post-facto AI review of the transcripts we identified opportunities to improve the follow-up question generation and ensure that grading only credited ideas that the student (and not the interviewer) contributed.

items.title: New AI agent observability and governance across BigQuery and Looker
items.summary:
As enterprises move AI agents from experimental prototypes into production, data and platform teams are discovering that deploying an agent is only half the battle — you also need to see how it reasons, which data it touches, and what it costs to run. Today, we are announcing expanded AI agent observability and evaluation capabilities across Google Data Cloud, giving you unified visibility into your first-party (1P) data agents in BigQuery and Looker as well as custom third-party (3P) agents built with agent development frameworks such as Agent Development Kit (ADK) or LangGraph.

Putting conversational and autonomous agents into production requires solving three operational challenges: tracing multi-step reasoning while protecting sensitive data, controlling token consumption and query spend, and evaluating answer accuracy before prompt or schema changes reach users. Let’s explore how our new agent observability and evaluation capabilities help you do this. 

What's new: Agent observability across Data Cloud

Running agents at scale means you need to see how they perform, what they cost, and what actions they take. We're rolling out a unified telemetry framework across Google's Agentic Data Cloud that works the same way for every agent: Capture telemetry from the agent, land it in BigQuery tables you own, and analyze it wherever your teams already work.

1. Capture telemetry from every first-party and custom agent

  • First-party data agents: Out-of-the-box Conversational Analytics agents emit telemetry automatically with no setup required. Queries routed to BigQuery data agents in Gemini Enterprise through agent-to-agent (A2A) workflows (now GA) send Cloud Monitoring metrics, Cloud Trace spans, and BigQuery conversation logs straight into your agent's project.

  • Custom agents: Agents built with ADK or LangGraph stream the same structured telemetry into BigQuery through single-line SDK instrumentation.

2. Land telemetry in one governed home in BigQuery

  • Conversation logging in BigQuery (GA): Managed 1P conversation logging writes to BigQuery tables you own, so you can inspect Conversational Analytics traces, including prompts and responses, directly in your data warehouse.

  • Governed by default: The Conversational Analytics API, now GA, includes always-on admin audit logs and optional data-read audit logs in Cloud Audit Logs, and supports VPC Service Controls, customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK), and regional and multi-regional data residency.

3. Analyze with dashboards wherever your teams work

  • In BigQuery (GA): Agent monitoring provides prebuilt dashboards in BigQuery Studio to track usage, active sessions, top knowledge sources, and latency across BigQuery Conversational Analytics agents.

  • In Looker (GA): System Activity dashboards for Conversational Analytics, now GA in Looker (Google Cloud core) and Looker (original), track engagement and token usage, while user ratings and query review in the Responses & feedback tab are in preview.
  • Build your own: Create interactive reports with the open-source Data Studio template or deploy the ready-made Looker Block for Agent Analytics for real-time custom agent monitoring.

Tracing agent reasoning and protecting privacy

Enterprise observability requires balancing diagnostic telemetry with strict data privacy boundaries. Because tracking features involve ingestion and storage costs, Google Data Cloud separates operational telemetry from conversation content so admins and agent owners can govern each layer independently.

At the project or organization level, admins can enable Cloud Monitoring (aggregate metrics such as request volume, latency, and token usage) and Cloud Trace (step-by-step spans for each request) across their environment, using Cloud Trace observability scopes to consolidate telemetry across multiple agent projects. To protect sensitive data, these operational metrics and sanitized first-party trace spans exclude customer core content (such as user prompts, model responses, internal thoughts, and generated SQL).

When you need deeper transcript auditing, agent owners and editors can opt in to conversation logging on a per-agent basis:

  • Governed conversation logging in BigQuery: When enabled, a Google-managed service agent streams user prompts, responses, and turn-level telemetry into a customer-owned BigQuery table (agent_events) via the BigQuery Storage Write API, inheriting your dataset's IAM permissions, CMEK, and VPC Service Controls. Built-in privacy guardrails enforce a fail-closed check before each turn — skipping logging whenever a knowledge source uses row-level security, column-level policy tags, or dynamic data masking — while fail-open execution keeps your users' chat sessions uninterrupted if a logging error occurs.

  • Full trace trees for custom 3P agents: While 1P conversation logging intentionally strips low-level tool arguments and internal SQL, developers building custom agents on ADK or LangGraph can instrument their code with the open-source ADK plugin (BigQueryAgentAnalyticsPlugin). With a single-line setup, the SDK streams full tool-invocation execution trees, time-series telemetry, and multimodal payloads straight into BigQuery.

  • In-warehouse root cause and drift analysis: Because conversation logs land natively in your agent_events table, you don't need separate export pipelines to diagnose failures. You can run BigQuery AI functions (such as AI.GENERATE to summarize error patterns and AI.EMBED with VECTOR_SEARCH to cluster recurring issues) or use the open-source bigquery-agent-analytics Python SDK and Colab starter notebook for post-hoc semantic drift clustering and LLM-as-a-judge sentiment analysis.

Controlling token costs with FinOps guardrails

As agent adoption grows, FinOps and platform teams need clear visibility into consumption alongside active controls to prevent runaway spend. With promotional trial pricing currently available for Conversational Analytics, now is a good time to establish baseline usage and cost guardrails:

  • Granular token and latency tracking: In BigQuery conversation logs, each turn records input, output, thought, cached, and total token counts alongside total turn latency, while Looker System Activity reports estimated input and output tokens across your business intelligence (BI) workloads.

  • Turnkey observability dashboards: You can track projected token usage and engagement in the BigQuery Studio Monitoring tab and native Looker System Activity dashboards, or query agent_events log data via BigQuery SQL using the open-source seven-page Data Studio report template and self-hosted Streamlit app in the BigQuery Agent Analytics GitHub repository.

  • Active query and token spend caps: To prevent unexpected charges before they happen, you can configure per-query BigQuery byte scan caps (big_query_max_billed_bytes) on your agent, which use dry-run estimates to block oversized queries without incurring on-demand scan charges. For BigQuery and the Conversational Analytics API, you can also enforce daily input and output token quotas (in preview) per project, user, or agent in the Google Cloud console and gcloud CLI.

Evaluating and benchmarking your AI agents

Runtime observability works alongside systematic evaluation. While logs and traces tell you how an agent behaved in production, evaluation benchmarks verify whether updates to your prompts, models, or data schemas improve SQL accuracy and answer quality before users experience a regression:

  • Benchmarking with Prism: Our open-source evaluation tool, Prism, lets you test Conversational Analytics agents grounded in BigQuery tables or Looker Explores via the Conversational Analytics API using reusable test suites, regex assertions, and multi-region agent discovery (deployed behind an access layer such as Cloud IAP).

  • Unified evaluation and production analytics: Prism can stream completed evaluation runs directly into day-partitioned BigQuery tables in your project, placing your pre-deployment benchmark scores right alongside your production agent_events logs for side-by-side analysis in BigQuery and Looker.

  • Native BigQuery evaluations: First-party agent evaluations in BigQuery (built on the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform evaluation service with bring-your-own-service-account support) are available in preview via API and a guided Colab notebook.

Getting started

Ready to bring visibility, governance, and cost control to your AI agents? Here is how to get started in three steps:

  1. Enable first-party agent observability. Turn on Cloud Monitoring and Cloud Trace in your project and opt in to per-agent conversation logging using the BigQuery agent monitoring guide, and track BI token consumption with the Looker Conversational Analytics overview and Looker System Activity documentation.

  2. Instrument custom agents and deploy analytics dashboards. Add the BigQuery Agent Analytics SDK to your ADK or LangGraph agents, launch the open-source Data Studio report template or Streamlit app, and explore in-warehouse log analysis with the Colab starter notebook.

  3. Benchmark your agents and set cost guardrails. Run automated accuracy suites with Prism, and configure BigQuery byte scan caps and daily token quotas via Manage BigQuery costs for agents.

items.story_key: story|title:what is eval driven development how to improve ai agents
items.content_excerpt: Development on most agents starts the same way. You write a prompt, try a few questions by hand, adjust, and try again. This works well in the beginning, when agent errors are obvious and improvements are easy to see. But over time it becomes increasingly difficult to know whether your most recent change made an agent better or worse. Eval-driven development (EDD) solves this by giving you a consistent set of metrics to measure your agent’s performance against and guide your decision making. Here at LangChain we've used EDD when building our most advanced agents (check out our blog on IssueBench ), and have boiled it down to a three step process: In this blog, we'll walk through this process step by step so that your team can apply it to your own agent development process. The name and concept of eval-driven development borrows from test-driven development (TDD), where you write a failing test before writing the code that passes it. Agents differ from traditional code as they're non-deterministic: As a result, agents need a different kind of test. An eval handles this by scoring runs of your agent across a set of examples. Evals are more flexible than traditional testing. You can score any aspect of the agent's run and you can use other LLMs to score it ( LLM-as-a-judge ). With EDD, similar to TDD, these evals become your definition of success and you build your agent towards them. The first step in EDD is defining what your agent should do. Then, list the behaviors it needs to handle to get there. These could be tasks such as answering questions from a knowledge base, taking an action on a user's behalf, or knowing when to ask a follow-up question. Write down the requirements for each behavior. Together, these make up a product requirements document (PRD) for your agent. EDD works on one behavior at a time. This gives you a narrow target to hill climb toward, without one change muddying the effect of another. The behavior you pick usually comes from a feature you're about to build or a failure you found in your agent's past runs. Before writing code, it’s helpful to define a short spec that covers: Say we have an internal docs agent that employees query for company information. It has two tools: search_docs for internal documentation and web_search for everything else. We plan to add a create_ticket tool so it can file IT tickets.
